The paper is rag: old linen shirts and sheets, beaten to pulp and lifted from the vat on a wire mould, which left the faint lines you see when a leaf is held up to the light.

A Garden of Flowers

with an account of each: its country, its uses, and its form.

The Spring, the Summer and the Autumn

Chap. I. Of the Eastern Hyacinth.

Hyacinthus orientalis.

The eastern hyacinth grows wild on stony hillsides in Syria, Lebanon and the south of Turkey, where it is a small, loose thing with a few pale blue bells. It came west from Con­stan­ti­no­ple in the sixteenth century, in the same bundles as the tulip, and the gardeners of the north have been fattening it ever since. The first here is double, its bells crowded one inside another.

The scent is the strongest of the spring: one spike will fill a room, and a bed of them on a warm evening can be smelled from the road. The bulb is round and purple-skinned; lift it when the leaves die down, dry it in the shade, and set it again in October four fingers deep. The sap makes the hands itch. The boy of the Greek story, killed by a discus, gave his name to a flower marked AI, AI, for grief. This is not that flower and has no such letters, but it took the name and has kept it.

In Holland they are grown by the acre in the sand behind the dunes, and the bulbs are sold by the hundred in autumn. A bulb set on the neck of a glass of water and kept in a dark cupboard will make roots like white string, and flower indoors in the middle of winter. After flowering, feed the bulb and let the leaves yellow of themselves: cut green, they starve it for the next year.

Chap. II. Of the Tulip.

Tulipa Turcarum.

The Turks grew tulips long before Europe did, and our word for the flower comes from theirs for a turban, by a traveller’s mistake. Conrad Gesner saw the first one in the West in a garden at Augsburg in April 1559: red, single, and with a scent he called sweet and soft. It has no virtue in medicine. The bulb can be eaten, and in the hunger winter of 1944 the Dutch ate them boiled.

Its whole worth is the colour. Now and then a plain red or yellow flower breaks, as the growers say, into flames and feathers, and no two broken flowers are alike. For three hundred years the best of them fetched the highest prices, and nobody knew that the breaking is a virus, carried from bulb to bulb by greenfly, which weakens the plant a little more every year. Plant in November in light, poor ground, a hand deep, and lift when the stalk is dry.

The flower opens wide in the warmth of noon and closes again toward evening, and when its time is over the petals fall all at once, cleanly. The wild ones are smaller, red or yellow, from the mountains of Central Asia, and come up in the same places for a hundred years. Mice and grey mould are its enemies; keep the lifted bulbs dry and cool through the summer, and look them over before they go back in.

Chap. III. Of the Marsh Marigold.

Caltha palustris.

It grows where the ground is always wet: in ditches and alder carr, along slow streams and in the hollows of water meadows, from Ireland to Kam­chat­ka and across the north of America. It is among the oldest flowers of these countries, and was here at the edge of the ice. The flower is a cup of five gold sepals and no petals at all, so glossy that it looks wet in the sun; the leaves are round and scalloped at the edge.

In Ireland and the Isle of Man it was hung over the door on May Eve to keep witches from the house. Every part is sharp and blistering when fresh, and cattle leave it standing in a grazed field; the buds, boiled, were once pickled in vinegar like capers. The double kind figured here sets little seed and is kept by dividing the roots. Give it mud, and it wants nothing else.

It flowers in March and April, before the grass is up, so that a wet meadow turns gold from one end to the other in a week. The country names, kingcup and mayblob and mollyblob, are all for that gold. It does best with its feet in water and its head in the sun, and spreads slowly into a clump that can be lifted and divided after it flowers.

Chap. IIII. Of the Stinking Gladdon.

Spatula foetida.

Gladdon grows in the shade of woods and on chalky hedge banks in the south of England, and across the west of Europe into Africa. Bruise a leaf and it smells: of roast beef, some say, and most say of something worse. The leaves are dark, evergreen and shaped like sword blades, which gives the Latin name. The flowers of June are small and dull, a grey violet netted with darker veins, and easy to pass by.

The plant keeps its show for autumn. Then the fat green pods split in three and fold back, and inside are rows of seeds as round and orange-red as coral beads, which hold on through the whole winter, after every other colour in the wood is gone. The root was boiled in ale as a purge, and is violent; it is better left alone. The seeds are good in a jug of winter berries.

It is one of only two irises that are native to Britain; the other is the yellow flag of the riverbanks. It will grow in dry shade under trees, where almost nothing else will, and that is the best reason to plant it. The split pods, cut and brought indoors, keep their seeds for weeks in a dry jug.

Chap. V. Of the Snapdragon.

Antirrhinum.

It is a plant of the dry Med­i­ter­ra­ne­an, at home in cracks of rock in Spain and the south of France, and it has settled on old walls wherever it has been carried, high up in the mortar where nothing else will take. The Greek name means like a snout. Pinch the sides of the flower and the mouth opens and shuts; children have always done it.

The mouth is shut on purpose. A bee must be heavy enough to press down the lower lip and push its way in, so only the big bumblebees reach the nectar, and they come out with pollen on their backs; smaller insects are kept out. It was hung in the house against en­chant­ment. It comes in red, white, yellow and the colour of old brick, and seeds itself where it pleases. Sow it on a wall and leave it.

In a garden it is a short-lived perennial, best grown as an annual: sow in late summer for flowers the next June, and pinch out the tops to make it bushy. The French call it gueule-de-loup, the wolf’s jaw, and English children call it lion’s mouth. In a wet summer rust spots the leaves; pull those plants out, and sow fresh ones somewhere else the next year.

Chap. VI. Of Birthwort.

Aristolochia.

Its name is Greek for the best of births. The flower is a long yellow tube swelling at the base, and by the old rule that a plant shows on its face what it is good for, the shape told physicians it belonged to childbirth; for two thousand years it was given to women in labour to bring away the afterbirth. The round kind has a root like a brown stone.

The flower is a trap. Small flies crawl down the tube and cannot climb back past the hairs that point inward; they are kept overnight until the flower sheds its pollen on them, and then the hairs wither and let them go. It grows in vineyards and stony places in the south, and in England most often by the ruins of nunneries, where it was planted. The leaves are heart-shaped and smell rank when bruised, and the festoon butterflies of the south lay their eggs on nothing else, so that their caterpillars carry its poison and the birds leave them alone. We know now that it poisons the kidneys slowly and causes cancers years after. Grow it for the flower, and take nothing from it.

Chap. VII. Of the Flower of the Sun.

Flos Solis maior.

It came from the Americas, where it had been grown for its seed for thousands of years, and reached Spain in the sixteenth century. Gerard heard of one twenty-four feet high in the royal garden at Madrid, and grew it fourteen feet in his own at Holborn. The head is as wide as a dinner plate and ringed with yellow rays; the middle is a thousand small flowers set in two sets of spirals turning against each other, thirty-four one way and fifty-five the other.

Young plants turn their heads after the sun from east to west, and back again in the night; when they flower they stop, and face the morning. The buds, boiled before they open and eaten with butter and vinegar like artichokes, Gerard thought exceeding pleasant meat. The seeds feed birds, hens and people, and press to a sweet oil.

Sow it in April against a warm wall, a foot apart, and stake the stems before July. One head will give a thousand seeds, and the birds will have every one of them unless the heads are cut first and hung to dry in an airy shed.

Chap. VIII. Of the Potato of Peru.

Papas Peruanorum.

It comes from the high Andes, where it is grown on terraces above the height of any grain, and where the frost of the nights is used to freeze-dry it into chuño that keeps for years. The Spaniards brought it home in the 1570s, and it passed from hand to hand among botanists; Clusius grew it in Vienna from two tubers sent him in 1588, and Gerard had himself engraved holding a sprig of its flowers.

Those flowers are white or lilac stars with a yellow beak, a nightshade’s, for it is one. The leaves, the green berries, and any tuber turned green by the light are poisonous; the tubers themselves, boiled or roasted in the embers, are wholesome and filling. Set them in spring in deep, loose ground, earth them up as the stems grow, and lift them when the haulm dies down. In the year of this book it was a curiosity, grown for its flowers. Within two hundred years whole countries lived on it, and when the blight came to Ireland in 1845 a million people died.

The garden these flowers were drawn from was laid out in terraces on the walls of the Willibaldsburg above Eichstätt, for the Prince-Bishop Johann Konrad von Gemmingen, who sent cut flowers to Nuremberg in boxes, week after week through three seasons, to be drawn. He died in 1612, the year before the book was finished. Soldiers sacked the castle in 1634 and the garden went with it; the copper plates outlasted it by almost two centuries, until they were melted down for their metal. What is left of the garden is the book.

Finis.

The plates were printed in black from copper and painted afterwards by hand, copy by copy, so no two books are quite alike: in one the tulip is flamed with crimson, in another with purple, and a colourist with the living flower in front of him worked differently from one copying a neighbour’s book. These leaves come from several copies, coloured in different workshops, bound here into one.

# page-turn An old printed herbal lying open, and you turn its leaves. Each leaf is a sheet of rag paper: take it by its edge or a corner and it bends from where you hold it, a curl that walks toward the spine as you lift, catching the light along its curve and falling into its own shade on the far side. Its shadow lies soft on the page beneath and spreads as the leaf rises. Held up against the light, the paper lets the print on its back show through, mirrored, with the chain lines of the papermaker's mould. Let go past the spine and it falls over, the trailing edge bowed back by the air, and settles on a cushion of air; let go before and it falls back; a flick turns it. The text pages are set with [pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext) (Cheng Lou): a running head, a chapter heading, a red drop cap the first three lines flow around, and justified paragraphs in the Fell types, about 26 lines to the page as an old herbal has, hyphenated by TeX's patterns so the word spaces stay even. The plates are hand-coloured engravings from Basilius Besler's *Hortus Eystettensis* (1613). ```html

A Garden of Flowers

with an account of each: its country, its uses, and its form.

Chap. II. Of the Tulip.

Tulipa Turcarum.

The Turks grew tulips long before Europe did, …

Its whole worth is the colour. …

…

The garden these flowers were drawn from …

``` The `
`s are the pages in reading order, and the first is a recto. On a wide screen they lie open in spreads: article 0 on the first right-hand page, then 1 and 2 facing, 3 and 4, and so on, so text pages (odd) fall on the left and plates (even) on the right. Below `data-single` px the book shows one page at a time, inset in its column with boards on both sides and only a sliver of the facing page at the spine; a turned leaf sweeps off the screen. You can also call `pageTurn(el, options)`; it returns `destroy()`. - A text page: `data-head` is the running head; `h2 > span` is the chapter line, the rest of the `h2` the heading; `.pt-latin` the Latin name in red; every other `

` is body text. The first paragraph opens with a three-line drop cap. Body text is hyphenated automatically (every word of six letters or more, Liang's algorithm with Knuth's US English patterns in `vendor/hyphen`, two letters before a break and three after); `­` you write yourself is kept. - `.pt-title`: each `span` in the `h1` is a line of big capitals; each `p` a block of italic lines (one per `span`); the last `p` sits at the foot in spaced small capitals. - `.pt-plate`: the image is printed onto the page inside its margins, with `multiply`, as an engraving is printed onto a sheet: prepare it as an ink layer on white (the scan's own paper divided out, its edges feathered to white), so every page in the book shares one paper and no rectangle shows. Any proportions; give it real `width`/`height`. - `.pt-colophon`: body text without a drop cap; `.pt-finis` is set in spaced capitals after it. - The page is sized to fit 84% of the viewport's height (74% for a single page), and the type is sized to the page (a 34th of its width on a 1.3 leading, made a little smaller only if a page's text would run over), so the pages have the same line breaks at every size. About 220 to 240 words fill a text page. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-start` | `start` | `1` | the spread to open at (0 is the title page alone on the right) | | `data-single` | `single` | `640` | below this container width (px), one page at a time | | `data-focal` | `focal` | `4.2` | camera height above the book, in page widths. Lower is stronger perspective: a lifted leaf grows more as it comes up toward you | The options object wins over the attributes. The book fires a `pageturn` event (`detail: { turned, leaves }`) on its element each time a leaf comes to rest on the other side or back where it was. ## How it works - **The leaf.** In its own frame (x out from the spine, y down the page) each point is measured along a direction *n* (s) and across it (t). Paper with s short of the fold line lies on the page; beyond it the sheet bends round a cylinder of radius R through an angle α and then runs straight. The bend's generators stay parallel to the fold, so the surface is developable and the paper never stretches (the cylinder construction of the classic page-curl papers). Two refinements make it paper rather than plastic: the bend radius grows away from the held point, so the far corner lags and the curl is conical, as when you pull a real corner; and the fold walks from the held point toward the spine as the leaf lifts (a corner peels first, then the whole leaf rises from the gutter), with the bend tightening to nothing as it lands. It is evaluated per vertex on an 85 × 101 grid in the vertex shader. - **Holding it.** A drag fixes *n* along the pull and solves, by bisection on a monotone function, for the lift that carries the held point exactly that far toward the spine. The held point is then up in the air, so the solve is repeated three times along the pointer's perspective ray until the paper is under the finger. On a single page the drag is geared 2.1 : 1, so a swipe across the page turns it. - **Letting go.** The turn becomes one number, u (0 lying right, 1 lying left), and the leaf a little dynamical system: gravity's torque on the share of the sheet that is lifted (∝ cos α), linear and quadratic air drag, and an air cushion that brakes the last 14% so it lands softly instead of slapping. The fold swings parallel to the spine, the cone relaxes, and a curvature on the free part follows the motion: it bows back against the air while it falls and droops under its own weight when it is slow. Past the spine it falls over, short of it it falls back, and a flick (more than 1.4 turns a second) is given enough speed to go over. Steps at 240 Hz. Up to three leaves can be in the air at once; a key pressed during a turn starts the next leaf. - **Keys.** ← and → (and Page Up / Page Down) turn a leaf by the same physics: a virtual hand takes the lower outer corner, lifts it along a short arc for 0.6 s and lets go just past the vertical; the whole turn takes about 0.9 s. Home and End go to the covers. The two small buttons under the book do the same. - **Light.** A soft window light from the upper left. Diffuse is wrapped and normalised (with a hemisphere term for the room), so a page lying flat shows its print exactly and only a bent one changes. A broad, faint sheen runs along the bend where it turns toward the light. The underside of a curl gets light thrown back from the paper below, warm, so the shade is never grey. - **Through the paper.** Lying flat, each page shows a 2.4% ghost of the print on its other side, softened by a blurred mip. Lifted, light reaching the far side passes through (7.5% translucency): the other side's print, mirrored, multiplied by this side's, and modulated by chain lines (every 1/11.5 of the page, vertical as in a folio) and laid lines (which fade out before they can alias). - **Shadow.** Every moving leaf is projected onto the table along the light by its height into a half-size buffer, as two channels: a contact term that dies off within about 5% of a page width of height, and a lift term that grows with height. They are blurred separately (narrow and wide, two separable passes) and laid on the pages, the page-block edges and the table, and on the part of the leaf still lying down, so the curl shades its own page. - **The book.** Pages dip into the gutter (5% of a page width deep), shaded by their slope and darkened toward the binding; the leaves underneath show as stepped page edges at the fore-edge, head and tail, thicker on whichever side has more of the book; sprinkled calf boards with worn edges; the book's own soft shadow on the table. - **Pages.** Each text page is a canvas: rag-paper ground (the plates' cream, clouded at three scales as hand-made paper settles on the mould, toned at the fore-edge and head, a few spots of foxing and fibres, seeded per page so each is different), then the type, word by word, each word inked a touch differently. pretext's `prepareWithSegments` and `layoutNextLine` give the breaks with a per-line width (the drop cap's indent) and honour the soft hyphens. Lines are broken 0.9% wider than the measure, so spaces may shrink a little as a compositor's would; a line is justified by stretching its spaces to at most 1.4 times, then by up to 0.02 em of letter-spacing, and only then (rarely, after hyphenation) by spaces wider still. Plates are the prepared scans printed with `multiply` onto that paper inside the margins. Textures are made on demand around the open spread and twelve are kept (mipmapped, anisotropic), about 1.08 × device pixels at DPR ≤ 2. ## Tuning The constants at the top of `page-turn.js`: `R0` (bend radius of a lifted leaf; bigger is stiffer paper), `CONE` (how much the far corner lags), `GUT_G` and `GUT_W` (gutter depth and width), `TRANS` (translucency when lifted), `GHOST` (show-through lying flat), `GRAV`, `DRAG1`, `DRAG2` (how fast it falls and how much the air holds it), `L` (the light). The lift profile is the `smooth(0.15, 1.75, alpha)` in `fam()`: move it right and a corner curls further before the whole leaf rises. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--pt-font` | IM Fell English | body text and italics | | `--pt-font-sc` | IM Fell English SC | running heads, the imprint | | `--pt-font-display` | IM Fell French Canon | headings, title, drop caps | | `--pt-paper`, `--pt-ink`, `--pt-rubric` | cream, warm black, madder | the no-script pages | | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | The Fell types are Igino Marini's revivals of the types Bishop John Fell gave to Oxford in the 1670s, on Google Fonts. On the canvas the ink is `#1e1914` and the rubric `#8f2c1c`; the paper colour is `PAPER` in the script (the plates were normalised to it). ## Behaviour and cost - Nothing runs while the book is still. A frame loop runs only while a leaf is in the air or a crossfade is running, and stops off screen and in a hidden tab. A drag redraws on pointer moves. - A frame is three small passes: the shadow (half size, ≤ 3 leaves of 17k triangles), four blur passes, the book quad, and the leaves. - The canvas reaches past the book (17% of a page above and below, sideways to the viewport's edge on a phone) so a leaf can rise out of it. DPR capped at 2, except a single page on a 3× phone, where the canvas (under 4.2 megapixels) and the page textures go to 3 because the type there is about 10 px and needs it. - Built when it comes within 600 px of the viewport, after the fonts have loaded. A resize settles any leaf in the air and re-sets the pages. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The articles stay in the DOM, visually hidden, as what screen readers read, find-in-page searches and print uses. The canvas is `aria-hidden`. The book is a focusable region (`aria-roledescription="book"`); ← → turn; a polite live region says which pages are open ("Pages 4 and 5 of 18: Of the Tulip, with its plate"). Two small, quiet buttons under the book turn back and forward. - Phones: `touch-action: pan-y`, so a vertical swipe scrolls the page; a sideways drag turns. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: a turn (key, button or swipe) is a 0.3 s crossfade of the open pages; nothing moves by itself. - Without JS or WebGL2: the pages one after another, text on paper cards and plates as images. ## Credits - [pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext) by Cheng Lou, MIT (`vendor/pretext`, unmodified, with its `LICENSE` and `VERSION`). - Hyphenation patterns: Knuth's `hyphen.tex` with the TUGboat exceptions, as `hyph_en_US.dic` from LibreOffice's dictionaries (unlimited copying and redistribution permitted); `vendor/hyphen/en-us.js` keeps the plain a-z patterns, with `LICENSE` and `VERSION`. - Plates: Basilius Besler, *Hortus Eystettensis* (Nuremberg, 1613; the sunflower from the 1713 edition), hand-coloured copies, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Each was flattened to an ink layer (its paper divided out, uneven light evened, edges feathered) by a script outside the component. See `assets/credits.json`. - The text was written for this component. - The page model follows the cylinder construction of the page-curl literature and Hong et al., *Turning Pages of 3D Electronic Books* (2006), for the cone; no code is taken from either.

hyph_en_US.dic - American English hyphenation patterns for OpenOffice.org

version 2011-10-07

- remove unnecessary parts for the new Hyphen 2.8.2

version 2010-03-16

Changes

- forbid hyphenation at 1-character distances from dashes (eg. ad=d-on)
  and at the dashes (fix for OpenOffice.org 3.2)
- set correct LEFTHYPHENMIN = 2, RIGHTHYPHENMIN = 3
- handle apostrophes (forbid *o'=clock etc.)
- set COMPOUNDLEFTHYPHENMIN, COMPOUNDRIGHTHYPHENMIN values
- UTF-8 encoding
- Unicode ligature support
